newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN health body launches West Africa cholera plan.
newsitem.headline: UN health body launches West Africa cholera plan.

text.p: The World Health Organisation said on Thursday it was launching a new drive to fight an explosion of cholera in West Africa, where the disease has spread rapidly in the past three years.
The United Nations agency said it was jointly funding the programme -- to be implemented in partnership with national health ministries -- together with a special grant from the Swiss government.
"The incidence of cholera has risen dramatically throughout West Africa in recent years," a statement from the WHO's Geneva headquarters said.
Of the 16 countries in the new project, only six had reported the disease in 1993 but this year there had been cases in 13 of them.

The annual number of cases in the region had exploded from a total of only 7,000 in 1993 to 42,500 in the first nine months of this year, and fatalities had seen a nine-fold increase -- from 369 in 1993 to more than 2,900 so far this year.
The West African region now accounted for two-thirds of all cholera cases on the continent and more than 70 per cent of all deaths there from the disease.
The 16 countries involved in the project are Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Ivory Coast, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo.

The WHO said a main aim of the drive would be to improve the region's capacity for a rapid response to cholera outbreaks and for treatment of individual cases. The average fatality rate for all 16 countries was currently running at six per cent.
"The project will also seek to improve the capacity of participating countries to develop and implement a common policy for epidemic preparedness and control," the WHO declared.
"It will stress food safety, health education for better hygiene in the home and the workplace, provision and use of safe water, and access to sanitation facilities."
An earlier anti-cholera project launched by the WHO in six countries of Southern Africa in 1993 has reduced the average annual case total from more than 57,000 to fewer than 1,500, the agency said.
